column3: 1. Does prohibition of use of force apply to cyber operations?
column4: 1.1 Can a stand-alone cyber operation violate the prohibition on the use of force?
column5: 2. Must a State intend for a cyber operation to amount to a use of force for there to be a violation of the prohibition on the use of force?
column6: 2.1 Must the cyber operation have a coercive character (or effect) to qualify as a use of force?
column7: 3. Does the State apply a “scale and effects” test to assess whether an action constitutes a use of force?
column8: 4. Does the state apply a totality of circumstances or similar context-based test to assess uses of force?
column9: 5. Does the state weigh the actual consequences of an action to assess whether it amounts to a use of force?
column10: 6. Does the State only recognize a use of force in cyber contexts by analogy to consequences caused by kinetic force (e.g., injury, death, damage or destruction)?
column11: 6.1 Are kinetic-like effects a required consequence of a cyber operation to qualify as a use of force (versus a factor among others to be considered)?
column12: 6.2 Does the State recognize a “small” or de minimus effects exception to the prohibition on the use of force?
column13: 6.3 Can non-violent effects alone qualify as “force” (e.g., substantial economic harm, losses of functionality, etc.)?
column14: 6.4 Can spill over effects from a cyber operation (i.e., those that are secondary or knock-on from the immediate effects) qualify as a use of force?
column15: 7. Does the State recognize an accumulation theory or similar aggregation theory of use of force?
column16: 8. Does the State consider a use of force to be the equivalent of an armed attack (per Article 51 of the UN Charter) subject to the same threshold?
column17: 9. Can a cyber operation amount to a prohibited threat of a use of force?
